29 A parallel beam of light consists of light of wavelength 420 nm and light of wavelength 630 nm.
The light is incident normally on a diffraction grating.
The diffraction maxima for the two wavelengths overlap only at an angle of 31 from the direction
of the incident light beam.
What could be the line spacing of the diffraction grating?
A
1.2 m
B
1.6 m
C
2.4 m
D
3.7 m

hints: Notice the two wavelengths $420 \text{nm}$ and $630 \text{nm}$ have ratio $630/420 = 1.5$, so overlapping orders must satisfy $n_{420} \times 420 = n_{630} \times 630$.
Recall the grating equation $d \sin \theta = n\lambda$ must give the same $d \sin 31^\circ$ for both colours with integer orders.
Try the smallest integers with ratio 3 to 2, then calculate $d = n\lambda / \sin 31^\circ$ and convert $\text{nm}$ to $\mu\text{m}$.
walkthrough: Write the grating equation for each wavelength at the same angle $\theta = 31^\circ$: $d \sin 31^\circ = n_1 \times 420 \text{nm}$ and $d \sin 31^\circ = n_2 \times 630 \text{nm}$.
For overlap, $n_1 \times 420 \text{nm} = n_2 \times 630 \text{nm}$, so $n_1/n_2 = 630/420 = 3/2$. The smallest integers are $n_1 = 3$ for $420 \text{nm}$ and $n_2 = 2$ for $630 \text{nm}$.
Calculate the common path difference: $n\lambda = 3 \times 420 \text{nm} = 1260 \text{nm}$, which also equals $2 \times 630 \text{nm} = 1260 \text{nm}$.
Convert to micrometres: $2450 \text{nm} = 2.45 \mu\text{m} \approx 2.4 \mu\text{m}$. This is option C.

A.explanation: About half of $2.4 \mu\text{m}$. It would give $d \sin 31^\circ$ about $620 \text{nm}$, which does not equal an integer multiple of both $420 \text{nm}$ and $630 \text{nm}$.

B.explanation: It gives $d \sin 31^\circ$ about $824 \text{nm}$, which is close to $2 \times 420 \text{nm}$ but is not an integer multiple of $630 \text{nm}$.

D.explanation: It gives $d \sin 31^\circ$ about $1900 \text{nm}$, which is $3 \times 630 \text{nm}$ but is not an integer multiple of $420 \text{nm}$.
